Content: Tables and graphs provide visual representations for situations described by linear functions, allowing us to see the structure of algebraic relationships. While an equation gives us a mathematical description of a function, tables and graphs provide us with data points that form a pattern of how a function behaves. A table organizes data into a neat list of inputs and outputs, allowing you to spot numerical trends from one row to the next. A graph transforms input-output pairs into a line that connects many points on the coordinate plane. In fields like engineering and economics, the ability to create trend line from individual data points is useful for visualizing patterns and predicting unknown outcomes for entirely new inputs.

Mastering the interplay between tables and graphs is incredibly useful because SAT problems frequently ask you to translate a function from one format to another. We might be given a table of values and asked to identify its corresponding graph, or given a graph and asked to find the matching algebraic equation. Because a straight line behaves identically whether it is written as a formula, graphed on a plane, or listed as data points in a table, learning how to read different formats lets us verify our answers. When unsure of our algebra, the graph or table can often be a simple path to finding the solution visually.

The golden thread that connects equations, tables, and graphs is the rate of change. The rate of change measures how fast the output (`y`) changes relative to a change in the input (`x`). On a graph, the rate of change is the “rise over run” — the steepness and direction of the line. In a table, the rate of change is the constant pattern you see as you move from one row to the next. For a function to be linear, this rate of change must be constant. If every time your input increases by `1`, your output increases by exactly `3`, you have a constant rate of change of `3`, which will result in particular steepness when the line is graphed.

When solving SAT problems, understanding the role of the rate of change is your ultimate shortcut. The test will often give you a table with just two or three coordinate points, such as `(2,5)` and `(4,11)`. By calculating the rate of change — subtracting the outputs divided by the subtraction of the inputs: `(11-5)(4-2)=6/2=3` — you can identify a key feature of the line. Once you calculate the rate of change, you can immediately eliminate any functions that don't include the correct number as the coefficient for `x`. By forcing yourself to look for the rate of change first, you can dismantle complex table or graph problems and even forecast input-output pairs that weren't given.
